Bayesian estimation of the accuracy of diagnostic tests

Source: R/fit.R
baysesp.Rd

Fits a Bayesian model for the sensitivity and specificity of one or more binary tests when not all subjects have been verified with the reference standard (Baker, 1995; Buzoianu and Kadane, 2008; Martinez et al., 2006). The objects of the model classes passed to model contain the specification of the priors and of the verification mechanism.

Usage

baysesp(
  data,
  model = saturated(),
  backend = c("rstan", "cmdstanr"),
  chains = 4,
  iter_warmup = 1000,
  iter_sampling = 1000,
  seed = NULL,
  ...
)

Arguments

data

A baysesp_data object, created by baysesp_data(), with the results of the tests, the verification indicator and the disease status of each subject. Any other object gives an error.

model

An accuracy model: an object created by one of the model constructors saturated(), loglinear() or random_effects(). It holds the priors on the model parameters and the verification mechanism, which is verification = mar() or verification = mnar() given to the constructor. Default saturated(), with MAR verification. Any other object gives an error.

backend

Stan interface, a single value: "rstan" (default) or "cmdstanr". With "rstan" (Stan Development Team, 2025), the Stan programs are the ones compiled when the package is installed, so nothing is compiled at run time. With "cmdstanr", each program is compiled the first time it is used and the executable is kept in the user cache directory, so the first run is slower and later runs reuse the compiled program. If cmdstanr or CmdStan is not available, "rstan" is used and a message is printed. The backend element of the result reports the backend that was actually used. Any other value gives an error.

chains

Positive integer, the number of Markov chains, which run independently. Default 4.

iter_warmup

Positive integer, the number of warmup iterations of each chain. The warmup iterations adapt the sampler and are then discarded. Default 1000.

iter_sampling

Positive integer, the number of sampling iterations of each chain, kept as draws. Default 1000, which gives chains * 1000 draws in total.

seed

NULL (default) or a single whole number between 0 and 2147483647. If NULL, a seed is drawn from the random number generator of R, so that calling set.seed() before baysesp() makes the run reproducible. A number is used directly as the seed of the sampler.

...

Further arguments passed to rstan::sampling() when backend is "rstan" (for example cores, to run the chains in parallel, or control, for example list(adapt_delta = 0.95)), or to the $sample() method of cmdstanr when backend is "cmdstanr" (for example parallel_chains, or adapt_delta). With saturated() the target acceptance rate adapt_delta is 0.95 unless given here, instead of the Stan default 0.8: see the profile_prevalence_prior argument of saturated(). Do not repeat chains, iter_warmup, iter_sampling or seed, which baysesp() already passes to the backend.

Value

An object of class baysesp_fit with the following properties:

  • model: the model object given in model.

  • data: the baysesp_data object given in data.

  • draws: a posterior::draws_array with the sampling iterations only, that is iter_sampling iterations, chains chains and the variables listed below.

  • backend: the backend used, "rstan" or "cmdstanr".

  • stan_fit: the object returned by the backend: a stanfit object for "rstan", a CmdStanMCMC object for "cmdstanr".

  • settings: a list with chains, iter_warmup, iter_sampling, the seed actually used and the arguments given in .... update() reuses them to fit a different model to the same data.

The profiles are the \(J = 2^K\) response profiles of the \(K\) tests, indexed in binary order: profile \(j\) is the pattern of results with index \(j = 1 + \sum_k t_k 2^{k-1}\), where \(t_k = 1\) for a positive result on test \(k\) and \(t_k = 0\) otherwise. Profile 1 has all tests negative, and the first test changes fastest. The variables in draws are:

  • prevalence: the prevalence of the disease.

  • theta_healthy[j] and theta_diseased[j]: the probability of profile \(j\) among the healthy and among the diseased. Within each draw, each of the two sets sums to 1 over \(j\).

  • omega[j], v[j] and phi1[j], only for the saturated model: the probability of profile \(j\), the probability of verification given profile \(j\), and the probability of disease among the verified subjects with profile \(j\). v[j] and phi1[j] are 0 for profiles with no verified subjects.

  • q[b]: the prevalence of disease among the subjects with the \(b\)-th profile that has no verified subjects. Present only if some profile has no verified subjects.

  • beta: the log odds ratio of verification between diseased and healthy subjects with the same profile, present only with MNAR verification (Kosinski and Barnhart, 2003). Without by_profile = TRUE it is a single value. With by_profile = TRUE there is one value, named beta[i], for each profile with verified subjects, in binary order.

  • alpha[i], only for loglinear() and random_effects() with MNAR verification: the log odds of verification of the healthy subjects with the \(i\)-th profile that has verified subjects, in binary order.

Details

The posterior distribution of the parameters of model, given data, is approximated with the No-U-Turn sampler of Stan, a form of Hamiltonian Monte Carlo that adapts its step size and mass matrix during the warmup iterations (Carpenter et al., 2017). The likelihood and the priors are coded in a Stan program specific to the model class and to the verification mechanism. Each chain runs iter_warmup warmup iterations, which are discarded, followed by iter_sampling sampling iterations, which are kept as draws. The draws therefore form chains * iter_sampling joint samples of the parameters of the model, and every quantity reported by the package is computed from them.

References

Baker, S. G. (1995). Evaluating multiple diagnostic tests with partial verification. Biometrics, 51(1), 330–337. doi:10.2307/2533339

Buzoianu, M. and Kadane, J. B. (2008). Adjusting for verification bias in diagnostic test evaluation: A Bayesian approach. Statistics in Medicine, 27(13), 2453–2473. doi:10.1002/sim.3099

Carpenter, B., Gelman, A., Hoffman, M. D., Lee, D., Goodrich, B., Betancourt, M., Brubaker, M., Guo, J., Li, P. and Riddell, A. (2017). Stan: A probabilistic programming language. Journal of Statistical Software, 76(1), 1–32. doi:10.18637/jss.v076.i01

Kosinski, A. S. and Barnhart, H. X. (2003). Accounting for nonignorable verification bias in assessment of diagnostic tests. Biometrics, 59(1), 163–171. doi:10.1111/1541-0420.00019

Martinez, E. Z., Achcar, J. A. and Louzada-Neto, F. (2006). Estimators of sensitivity and specificity in the presence of verification bias: A Bayesian approach. Computational Statistics & Data Analysis, 51(2), 601–611. doi:10.1016/j.csda.2005.12.021

Stan Development Team (2025). RStan: The R interface to Stan. R package. https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=rstan

See also

test_accuracy()

Examples

# \donttest{
set.seed(1)
d <- simulate_study(n = 1000, prevalence = 0.2,
                    sensitivity = c(A = 0.9, B = 0.8),
                    specificity = c(A = 0.85, B = 0.95),
                    verification_prob = c(0.2, 0.9, 0.9, 1))
d <- baysesp_data(d, tests = c("A", "B"), verified = "verified", disease = "disease")
fit <- baysesp(d, seed = 1)
test_accuracy(fit)
#>     quantity      mean    median     lower     upper identified
#> 1 prevalence 0.2032967 0.2029564 0.1776183 0.2304198       TRUE
#> 2      Se[A] 0.8949437 0.8973944 0.8408835 0.9370849       TRUE
#> 3      Sp[A] 0.8497024 0.8498352 0.8236039 0.8748486       TRUE
#> 4     PPV[A] 0.6030221 0.6031086 0.5445309 0.6599996       TRUE
#> 5     NPV[A] 0.9693508 0.9702629 0.9513761 0.9822349       TRUE
#> 6      Se[B] 0.7975647 0.7987924 0.7329281 0.8545418       TRUE
#> 7      Sp[B] 0.9472373 0.9474472 0.9303955 0.9620185       TRUE
